attribution: Source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Underlying data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, Census Bureau, Federal Reserve Board, Freddie Mac and the NBER.

median_home_price.label: Median sales price of houses sold

card_rate.label: Average credit card interest rate, all accounts

gross_debt_dollars.label: Federal debt held by the public, dollars

tiles.title: Jobs added
tiles.subtitle: Nonfarm payrolls, change from the month before
tiles.note: Seasonally adjusted. The first two prints for any month are revised.

household.text: At this month's pace the economy adds about 348,000 jobs a year. The 2015–19 pace was about 2.3 million a year.

tiles.title: Unemployment rate
tiles.subtitle: Share of the labor force looking for work
tiles.note: Seasonally adjusted, from the monthly household survey.

household.text: About 7.2 million people are looking for work, one in 24 of everyone in the labor force.

tiles.title: New jobless claims
tiles.subtitle: First-time unemployment filings, 4-week average
tiles.note: Seasonally adjusted. Weekly, so it moves before the monthly jobs numbers do.

household.text: About 197,000 people filed for unemployment benefits in an average week, 20% below the 2015–19 norm of about 245,000.

tiles.title: Inflation
tiles.subtitle: Consumer prices, change from a year ago
tiles.note: All items, all urban consumers (CPI-U), seasonally adjusted.

source.fred_title: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average

household.text: What cost $100 a year ago costs $103.72 now. What cost $100 in 2019 costs $131.54.

tiles.title: Core inflation
tiles.subtitle: Consumer prices excluding food and energy, change from a year ago
tiles.note: Strips out the two most volatile groups to show the underlying trend.

source.fred_title: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items Less Food and Energy in U.S. City Average

household.text: Leaving out food and energy, what cost $100 a year ago costs $102.57 now.

tiles.title: Economic growth
tiles.subtitle: Real GDP, quarterly change at an annual rate
tiles.note: Inflation-adjusted. Each quarter is revised twice after its first estimate.

household.text: In the quarter itself the economy grew 0.8%; “3.4%” is that pace continued for a full year.

tiles.title: Fed funds rate
tiles.subtitle: The Federal Reserve's policy rate, monthly average
tiles.note: Effective rate: what banks actually paid to borrow overnight.

household.text: Money market funds and online savings follow it within days (3-month Treasury bills pay 4.0%); credit cards within a statement (the average card charges 21.2%); mortgages only through the 10-year yield.

tiles.title: 10-year Treasury yield
tiles.subtitle: What the U.S. government pays to borrow for ten years
tiles.note: History is the monthly average; the headline is the latest daily close.

source.fred_title: Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 10-Year Constant Maturity, Quoted on an Investment Basis

household.text: Borrowing $1,000 for ten years costs the Treasury $50 a year at this yield, $23 at the 2015–19 average. Mortgage rates run about 1.9 points above it.

tiles.title: Housing starts
tiles.subtitle: New homes begun, annual rate
tiles.note: Seasonally adjusted annual rate: the month's pace, if it continued all year.

source.fred_title: New Privately-Owned Housing Units Started: Total Units

household.text: At this pace, about 859,000 houses and 362,000 apartments get started in a year.

tiles.title: 30-year mortgage rate
tiles.subtitle: Average fixed rate on new mortgages, weekly
tiles.note: Freddie Mac's weekly survey of lenders.

source.fred_title: 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States

household.text: On the median home sold ($393,300), a mortgage with 20% down costs $2,161 a month at this rate, $1,925 at a year ago's rate, and $1,501 at the 2015–19 average. Principal and interest only.

tiles.title: Federal deficit
tiles.subtitle: What Washington borrowed in the fiscal year, as a share of the economy
tiles.note: Fiscal years end September 30. Negative is a deficit; the rare positive readings are surpluses.

source.fred_title: Federal Surplus or Deficit [-] as Percent of Gross Domestic Product

household.text: Of every dollar the government spent, about 25¢ was borrowed. The deficit was 5.8% of GDP; the 2015–19 average was 3.5%.

tiles.title: Federal debt
tiles.subtitle: Debt held by the public, as a share of the economy
tiles.note: Excludes the debt the government owes its own trust funds. The level, not the yearly change; the deficit is the change.

source.fred_title: Federal Debt Held by the Public as Percent of Gross Domestic Product

household.text: The debt held by the public comes to about $92,408 per person. Interest on it costs about 3.9% of GDP a year, roughly $3,790 per person.

tiles.title: Trade deficit
tiles.subtitle: Goods and services: exports minus imports, monthly
tiles.note: Seasonally adjusted. Negative means the country bought more from abroad than it sold.

source.fred_title: Trade Balance: Goods and Services, Balance of Payments Basis

household.text: At this month's pace the country buys about $3,692 more from abroad per person each year than it sells.
